questions.question: How many patients and how many centers does the updated REFINE SPECT registry include?
questions.expected_answer: 45,252 patients from 13 centers.

questions.question: Which events were counted as major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) in the registry?
questions.expected_answer: All-cause mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina, and late coronary revascularization.

questions.question: What degree of coronary stenosis was considered significant or obstructive on invasive angiography?
questions.expected_answer: At least 70% in the LAD, left circumflex or right coronary artery, or at least 50% in the left main coronary artery.

questions.question: How was coronary artery calcium scored from the CT attenuation scans, and how well did the deep learning scores agree with expert scores?
questions.expected_answer: Experts annotated CAC, and a deep learning model derived scores automatically; agreement with expert scores was good (Cohen kappa 0.80).

questions.question: How much higher was the risk of MACEs for patients with a deep learning coronary calcium score above 400?
questions.expected_answer: Unadjusted hazard ratio of 5.17 (95% CI 4.41-6.05) compared with a CAC of 0.

questions.question: What limitations does the REFINE SPECT registry have?
questions.expected_answer: Least-common-denominator data; visual stenosis assessment overestimates functionally significant disease versus fractional flow reserve; all-cause death used; heterogeneity between centers and interobserver variability.

questions.question: How long did batch processing of each patient case take?
questions.expected_answer: Approximately 2.1 seconds per complete patient case.

questions.question: How accurate was the AI system compared with cardiologists working with and without AI guidance?
questions.expected_answer: AI 88%, cardiologists with AI guidance 80%, cardiologists alone 65%.

questions.question: How did noise and artifacts in the images affect the performance of the diagnosis model?
questions.expected_answer: 14.2% of images contained artifacts; performance was much lower on them (AUC 0.74, AUPRC 0.78) than on non-artifact images (AUC 0.93, AUPRC 0.90).

questions.question: Which image axis gave the best performance when a model was trained on a single axis?
questions.expected_answer: The short axis (AUC 0.88, AUPRC 0.83).

questions.question: What neural network architecture was used, and how were the three image axes combined with the patient's age and sex?
questions.expected_answer: A 3D CNN based on ResNet-34 with three branches (one per axis) whose outputs are concatenated with age and sex before dense layers.

questions.question: How were the data divided into training, validation and test sets?
questions.expected_answer: 10% for testing and 10% of the rest for validation: 4356 training, 542 validation and 545 test cases.

questions.question: Which data augmentation techniques were applied to the SPECT images?
questions.expected_answer: Slight rotation (up to five degrees), brightness change, zooming and shifting; classes were augmented to 12,000 images each.

questions.question: What hardware and software environment was used to train the deep learning model?
questions.expected_answer: A server with two Quadro RTX8000 GPUs, using TensorFlow 2.4.0 and Python 3.7.7 in Docker.

questions.question: Why is it unclear whether the SPECT deep learning diagnosis system would work at other hospitals?
questions.expected_answer: The dataset was collected from a single center (Keio University).

questions.question: How many participants took part in the simultaneous EEG-fMRI evaluation, and how many were analysed for each task?
questions.expected_answer: Sixteen participants; 12 analysed for resting-state and visual evoked potentials and 13 for finger tapping.

questions.question: What are the main types of MR artifacts that contaminate EEG recorded inside the scanner?
questions.expected_answer: Imaging (gradient) artifacts, ballistocardiogram (BCG) artifacts, and vibration artifacts such as those from the helium pump.

questions.question: How does average artifact subtraction work, and what assumptions does it make?
questions.expected_answer: It averages the EEG over several periods to build an artifact template and subtracts it; it assumes the neural signal is uncorrelated across averaged epochs and the artifact is stationary.

questions.question: What is the carbon-wire loop method and how many loops does it use?
questions.expected_answer: A reference-signal method using six carbon-wire loops (four on the head, two on cables), isolated from the scalp; their signals and time-shifted copies are regressed out of the EEG.

questions.question: Which artifact reduction method best recovered alpha and beta band changes during finger tapping?
questions.expected_answer: The carbon-wire loop (CWL) method; no other method substantially improved the alpha or beta results.

questions.question: What do the authors recommend for EEG-fMRI studies where participants must make voluntary movements?
questions.expected_answer: Use a reference-signal-based artifact correction such as a carbon-wire loop system.

questions.question: Which probabilistic programming language was used to estimate the statistical models?
questions.expected_answer: Stan.
